text:
alex: Thinking out loud — should we rely on preemptible nodes for cost savings in Dedicated GPU pools, or implement priority classes + soft-eviction as the canonical autoscaler model? Pros/cons and interface boundaries?

maria: prefer priority classes + soft-eviction. Preemptible nodes are cheap but noisy: hard to guarantee latency SLOs for critical routes.

cheng: +1 to priority classes. Also we need a clear contract between allocator and autoscaler: allocator decides placement given a set of live nodes and priorities; autoscaler adjusts node counts and marks preemptible vs reserved.

sam: from an infra POV, preemptible instances are great for burst capacity. But we must ensure safe fallback (eg route traffic to reserved pool, not drop requests). That means autoscaler needs to expose "drain plan" semantics.

leah: product thought — customers on Dedicated expect SLAs. If we mix preemptible nodes into their default pool we need explicit opt-in and UI labels. No surprises.

alex: Thinking of a small API sketch for autoscaler policy. Something like: ```yaml
policy:
  priorities:
    - name: reserved
      min_instances: 4
      preemptible: false
      eviction_score: 100
    - name: best_effort
      min_instances: 0
      preemptible: true
      eviction_score: 10
  latency_target_ms: 120
  cost_weight: 0.3
  max_preemptible_fraction: 0.5
```

maria: That looks good. Important: eviction_score should be combined with runtime metrics (kv cache warmness, recent requests) — otherwise we'll evict hot containers and regress latency.

derek: For graceful preemption we need a short terminal window for reclaiming KV caches and transferring warmups. Maybe 30-60s drain plus option to snapshot KV to object store for fast warmups.

sam: We experimented with a "soft preempt" where the node is marked drainable and we stop new cheap workloads, keep warm state for in-flight / expected soon requests. Works for <2min windows.

cheng: Interface boundary idea: autoscaler only sets node metadata (priority_class, preemptible=true/false, drain_until_ts). Allocator subscribes to node-change events and enforces placement policy. Eviction decisions are computed by the autoscaler (it knows cost/latency tradeoffs) but actual process is performed by the node controller.

alex: So responsibilities: autoscaler = global optimization + policy; node controller = execution (cordon, drain, terminate); allocator = placement given current node inventory + priorities. Sounds cleaner.

maria: Agree. Also store the policy version in cluster state so we can do canary policy rollouts (apply to subset of pools first).

leah: Customer-facing controls: slider for preemptible fraction, toggle for allow_preemptibles, and SLA enforcement that will refuse to use preemptible nodes for routes marked "production-critical".

derek: Metrics to expose: preemptible_evictions/sec, average_drain_time, avg_kv_warmness_by_priority, requests_fallback_to_reserved. Also a per-route cost delta when preemptible fraction changes.

sam: Ops automation: when autoscaler decides to terminate preemptible nodes, autoscaler-bot will post a plan and wait 60s for manual abort in critical windows. Not automatic during high-incident windows.

autoscaler-bot: planned_scale: pool=dedicated-gpu-europe-west1, action=reduce_preemptible 8->4, reason=low_weekend_util, ETA=2026-07-14T02:03:40Z

alex: Long-term refactor: split autoscaler into two processes: planner (optimization with cost model + ML predictors) and executor (policy enforcement + safety checks). Planner can be heavier and async; executor must be fast and idempotent.

cheng: +1. Planner keeps historical models and can simulate upgrades. Executor exposes a minimal API: apply_scale(plan_id, node_changes[]). That will help audits.

maria: Couple of open questions: 1) Do we allow preemptible-only pools (customer opts in fully)? 2) How do we surface latency regressions due to eviction (automatic rollback threshold)?

leah: 1) yes, opt-in. We already have customers asking for a "spot-only" cheaper tier. 2) show realtime regression alerts in Console and auto revert policy if P95 latency increases > X% for Y minutes.

derek: Implementation note: ensure eviction_score calculation includes model-size and tokenizer cache size (big models are expensive to warm). Maybe prioritize evicting small-model workloads first.

alex: Ok action items: @maria to draft final policy YAML and eviction_score formula. @cheng to spec the planner/executor API. @sam to add ops-bot abort window + implementation notes. @leah to draft product control copy for Console. I'll follow up with a short RFC next week.

maria: I'll put a prototype policy in the repo by EOD tomorrow.

sam: I'll add the ops-bot patch to pause automated scale during incident-mode.

alex: Thanks all :thumbsup:
